meta.title: Clinical - العلاج الطبيعي للاضطرابات الجلدية - PT - Integumentary Disorders
meta.subject: الطب السريري

cards.q: What is the definition of an ulcer?
cards.a: A **break in the skin or mucous membrane** that fails to heal due to **poor circulation or pressure**.

cards.q: What are the common sites for pressure ulcers in a supine position?
cards.a: Sacrum, **heels**, occiput, **blades of scapulae**, and elbows.

cards.q: Name the common sites for pressure ulcers when in a side-lying position.
cards.a: Acromion, **greater trochanter**, femoral condyles, and **lateral malleolus**.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for pressure ulcer development?
cards.a: Immobility, **moisture**, friction & shear, **age**, and comorbidities like **D.M.**, **peripheral vascular disease**, and **hypotension**.

cards.q: Define Stage I pressure ulcer.
cards.a: Intact skin with **non-blanchable redness** of a localized area, usually over a bony prominence.

cards.q: Define Stage II pressure ulcer.
cards.a: Partial thickness loss of **dermis** presenting as a shallow open ulcer with a **red-pink wound bed**, without slough.

cards.q: Define Stage III pressure ulcer.
cards.a: Full thickness tissue loss where **subcutaneous fat** may be visible, but bone, tendon, or muscle are **not exposed**.

cards.q: Define Stage IV pressure ulcer.
cards.a: Full thickness tissue loss with **exposed bone, tendon, or muscle**; slough or eschar may be present.

cards.q: Define an Unstageable pressure ulcer.
cards.a: Full thickness tissue loss in which the base of the ulcer is covered by **slough (yellow, tan, gray, green, or brown) and/or eschar (tan, brown, or black)**.

cards.q: What are the causes of venous leg ulcers?
cards.a: Improper functioning of **venous valves** or **high venous blood pressure**.

cards.q: What is the primary cause of arterial (ischemic) ulcers?
cards.a: Poor **perfusion** to the lower extremities leading to **oxygen deprivation** and tissue death.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of neuropathic ulcers?
cards.a: Nerve damage, typically in people with **diabetes**, **peripheral neuropathy**, or **spinal cord injuries**.

cards.q: Which type of ulcer is the most common cause of lower extremity amputation in diabetic patients?
cards.a: **Diabetic ulcers**.

cards.q: List four characteristics of venous skin ulcers.
cards.a: Painless ulcers (above ankle), **pigmentation**, **eczema**, **ankle flare**, **varicose veins**, and **lipodermatosclerosis**.

cards.q: What is the 'clock face' orientation used for in wound assessment?
cards.a: Mapping the **anatomical location and dimensions** of an ulcer (e.g., describing tunneling or wound edges).

cards.q: Differentiate between tunneling and undermining.
cards.a: **Tunneling** is a channel extending from the wound into surrounding tissue; **undermining** is a separation of tissue underneath the wound edge forming a gap.

cards.q: What does the presence of granulation tissue indicate?
cards.a: A **positive sign of healing**, characterized by firm, red, pebbly, and moist tissue.

cards.q: Why must slough be removed from a wound?
cards.a: It is non-viable, yellowish/stringy tissue that can **impede healing and harbor bacteria**.

cards.q: How is necrotic tissue (eschar) described?
cards.a: Black, leathery, or hard dead tissue that must be **debrided** as it impedes healing.

cards.q: What are the four types of wound exudate?
cards.a: **Serous** (clear/watery), **serosanguineous** (thin/pink-tinged), **sanguineous** (blood-tinged), and **purulent** (thick/opaque/infected).

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of a foul smell in a wound?
cards.a: It often suggests **infection**.

cards.q: What are the signs of infection in the peri-wound skin?
cards.a: **Erythema** (redness), **warmth** (increased temperature), and **induration** (hardness/firmness).

cards.q: What is Maceration in the context of wound care?
cards.a: White, wrinkled, overly moist skin caused by **excessive exudate** or poor dressing management.

cards.q: How is Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) calculated?
cards.a: Divide **ankle pressure** by **arm pressure**.

cards.q: What is the normal ABI range?
What does an ABI <0.9 indicate?
cards.a: Suggests **arterial disease**; lower values indicate more severe **ischemia**.

cards.q: What does an ABI >1.4 indicate?
cards.a: **Non-compressible vessels**, common in diabetes or renal failure.

cards.q: What is the normal capillary refill time?
cards.a: **Less than 3 seconds**.

cards.q: What are the two major pressure ulcer risk assessment tools?
cards.a: The **Braden Scale** and the **Norton Scale**.

cards.q: What is the ideal negative pressure for NPWT (VAC therapy)?
List three contraindications for NPWT.
cards.a: Untreated osteomyelitis, **presence of necrotic tissue**, **malignancy in the wound**, **exposed organs/blood vessels**, or non-enteric fistula.

cards.q: What is the wavelength range of UV rays?
Which type of UV is highly antimicrobial for acute wound infections?
List three contraindications for UV therapy.
cards.a: Pulmonary tuberculosis, **severe cardiac disturbances**, **severe diabetes**, known photosensitivity, and acute febrile illness.

cards.q: What are the wavelengths used in Polarized Light Therapy (PLT)?
What is the primary function of keratinocytes?
cards.a: To form a **barrier** against environmental damage (bacteria, fungi, parasites, UV, etc.).

cards.q: What laser types are used for superficial wound healing?
cards.a: **He Ne laser** (5 J/cm2) and **Ga As diode laser** (3 J/cm2).

cards.q: Define Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT).
cards.a: Inhalation of **100% oxygen** within a chamber pressurized to **greater than 1 ATA**.

cards.q: What are the common parameters for High Voltage Pulsed Current (HVPC) wound treatment?
cards.a: 45 min/day, 3 days/week, **100 Hz frequency**, and use of **cathode** polarity to reduce bacteria.

cards.q: What pressure range do medical compression stockings provide at the ankle?
cards.a: **25 mmHg to 32 mmHg**.

cards.q: What is the recommended leg elevation for venous ulcer patients?
cards.a: Elevating the leg **above the level of the heart by 10–30°**.

cards.q: What is the most effective element of conservative leg ulcer treatment?
cards.a: Physical activity (**walking and exercise**) combined with **compression therapy**.
